A spouse made the other a joint holder of a pre-marital bank account shortly before marriage, which the husband later claimed as personal property under Art. 179(a) CC. The legal issue concerns whether the act of joint titling (co-intestazione) automatically transfers 50% ownership to the other spouse as an indirect donation. The Court applied the principle that joint holding only constitutes an indirect donation if an animus donandi (intent to give) is verified. In this case, the fact that the wife had resigned from her job to follow the husband abroad provided evidence of a reciprocal intent to share assets, thus the pre-marital sums became part of the common property.
A parent donated €40,000 to her son, which was immediately reinvested into securities within days of the deposit. The interpretative problem is whether such an indirect donation of securities is excluded from the community property under Art. 179(b) CC, or if it requires the formal declaration and spousal participation mandated by Art. 179(f) and para. 2 CC for purchases. The Court ruled that indirect donations fall under the exclusion of Art. 179(b) and do not require the formal adherence or declarations of the other spouse. Proven by the close timing between the donation and the investment, the securities were declared the husband's exclusive property.
A spouse received a cheque from a former employer and various sums from relatives as wedding gifts. The legal challenge involves distinguishing between personal assets excluded under Art. 179(e) CC and community property under Art. 177(a) CC. Regarding the employer's payment, the Court applied the principle that sums received as compensation for damage—rather than remuneration—are personal; the payment's timing after the termination of employment confirmed its compensatory nature. Conversely, wedding gifts intended for the couple's support fall into the community property. Since testimony confirmed the gifts were meant for both, those sums were divided equall.
